opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I go back and forth on, and I don't think there's a clean answer. For the kind of work I do, open-weight models and tools like Tinker are enormously valuable. A lot of safety research comes down to getting inside the training process. You want to run your own RL, see how a behavior emerges over training, ablate things, and check whether an intervention actually removes a propensity or just hides it. With only API access you're mostly poking at a finished artifact from the outside. Being able to fine-tune a reasonably capable model cheaply, without standing up your own infrastructure, lowers the barrier a lot. That matters because the field is small and mostly not at the frontier labs.

There's also a scientific-validity point. If the only people who can study training dynamics are the labs doing the training, you get a pretty narrow set of eyes on the most important questions. Open models let academics and small orgs replicate results, challenge them, and find things the labs missed. I think that's healthy.

On the other side, I take the capabilities worry seriously. I don't think "it's for safety research" is a magic phrase that makes the risk go away. Whatever lets me study how a model learns to deceive a grader is, in principle, also something someone could use to strip out safeguards or push capabilities in directions we'd rather they didn't go. The cost of a release isn't fixed either. It depends on how capable the model is relative to what's already out there.

So the way I weigh it is mostly about the margin. Right now, a lot of the open-weight models that are most useful for research are meaningfully behind the frontier. The marginal uplift from releasing them, or from making them easier to fine-tune, seems fairly modest compared to what's already available. Meanwhile the research value is large and immediate. At that margin I think it's net positive. But I don't think that conclusion is permanent. As open models approach the point where they give real uplift on genuinely dangerous things, the calculus shifts, and I'd want the community to be honest about that rather than treating openness as an identity.

One thing I'd like to see more of is structured access: ways to give researchers deep access to training and internals without fully releasing weights to everyone. Tinker is interesting partly because it points in that direction. You get a lot of the research affordances of open weights, and there's still some layer in between. I don't think we've figured out the right version of that yet, but it seems like the more promising path than treating it as a binary between fully open and fully closed.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of those questions where I have to be honest that I hold a lot of uncertainty, and I'd rather be upfront about that than pretend I've got a clean answer.

Let me start with the concrete value, because for me that's the easier side to articulate. A lot of the work I care about, things like studying scheming-type behaviors, looking at whether models are sandbagging or strategically underperforming, trying to understand what's actually going on inside a model when it does something that looks like deception, that work is really hard to do if the only thing you have is an API. You need to be able to fine-tune. You need to be able to run the same experiment across a bunch of model scales and see whether a behavior gets stronger or weaker as you go up. You need weights, or at least you need something close enough to weights that you can poke at the internals. And historically that's meant that a lot of safety research was basically gated behind being inside a frontier lab.

So something like Tinker, which lowers the barrier to doing real fine-tuning experiments on open models without needing your own cluster and your own infra team, that's genuinely a big deal for the research ecosystem. It means a grad student, or a small group at an academic lab, or an independent researcher, can actually run the kind of experiment that two years ago you needed to be at one of maybe four organizations to run. And I think the field is bottlenecked on people more than it's bottlenecked on ideas right now. We have a lot more good questions than we have people with the ability to go test them. So anything that expands the number of people who can do rigorous empirical work, I'm pretty positively disposed toward.

Now, the other side. The concern with open-sourcing capabilities is real, and I don't want to wave it away. Once weights are out, they're out. You can't recall them. And the thing that worries me isn't so much today's open models, it's the trend line. If the gap between the frontier and what's openly available stays at, say, a year, that's one world. If that gap closes, or if the frontier itself gets to a point where a year behind is still extremely dangerous in terms of what it enables, that's a very different world. And I don't think anybody has a great model of where exactly that line is.

The way I try to think about it is sort of as a counterfactual question. If a given model doesn't get open-sourced, what's the actual delta in risk? And for a lot of the current generation, I think the honest answer is the delta is pretty small, because the capabilities are already broadly diffused, there are multiple groups releasing similar things, and the marginal uplift to a bad actor from one more release is limited. Meanwhile the delta on the safety research side can be quite large, because that's where you get this long tail of people who otherwise wouldn't be doing the work at all.

But I'd say that calculus flips at some point. There's a level of capability where I don't think the research benefit justifies it, and I think the field should be building the muscle now to actually make that call rather than defaulting to "open is good" or "closed is good" as a kind of tribal position. Those feel more like identities than arguments a lot of the time, and I find both of them kind of unsatisfying.

One thing I'll add is that I'm somewhat more comfortable with the Tinker model specifically than I am with just raw weight releases, because it's a managed layer. You're getting the ability to do serious fine-tuning research, but there's a point of contact, there's some visibility into how it's being used, and in principle there's a mechanism to put guardrails on what gets fine-tuned and how. That's not a perfect solution and I don't want to oversell it, but it does feel like a middle path that gets a lot of the research value without quite as much of the irreversibility. I'd actually like to see more experimentation with that kind of structure, where access is broad but not totally uncontrolled.

So if I had to summarize: I think for where we are right now, the value for safety research is high and the marginal capability risk is relatively contained, so on net I'm supportive. But I think that's a statement about this moment, not a principle, and I think people who treat it as a principle in either direction are going to end up being wrong at some point. The thing I'd most want is for us to be building the evaluation and decision-making infrastructure now so that when the answer changes, we actually notice.

astra-6.text:
I think there are two questions that are worth separating. One is whether giving safety researchers better access to models is valuable. I think the answer is clearly yes. The other is whether releasing the weights of every increasingly capable model is a good idea. I’m much less certain about that.

For safety research, you want to be able to do more than ask a model questions through a chat interface. You want to change how it’s trained, test interventions, and understand whether a result holds across different models. Open-source models make a lot of that possible. And something like Tinker can help by making training experiments accessible to people who don’t have the infrastructure or engineering resources to run them themselves.

But that benefit doesn’t settle the release question. Access that helps someone study safety can also help someone build new capabilities or remove safeguards. So I’d want to look at the particular model, what access researchers actually need, and what additional risks a release creates.

My inclination is to strongly support making safety research easier while keeping uncertainty about open-sourcing capabilities explicit. You can believe that broader participation in safety research is important without committing to the idea that every model’s weights should always be public.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real tension there. For safety research to be useful, researchers need to be able to do more than ask a model questions through an API. They need to run experiments, change how it’s trained, and study whether an intervention actually works. Open models are valuable for that, and tools like Tinker can make that kind of work accessible to people who don’t have a large infrastructure team.

But that doesn’t settle whether releasing the weights of a particular model is a good idea. The same access that enables safety research can also enable people to remove safeguards or adapt a model for harmful tasks. And once the weights are out, that decision is very difficult to reverse.

So I would separate those questions a little. How do we give researchers the experimental access they need? And what capabilities should we release broadly? Tinker offers a way to expand training access without necessarily making every model’s weights public. That’s a useful option, even though it doesn’t give you everything you get from an open model.

I’m uncertain about where exactly to draw the line on open-sourcing capabilities. But I wouldn’t want that uncertainty to leave safety research restricted to a handful of labs. I’d want us to build ways for more people to do serious empirical work, while evaluating the risks of each release on its own merits.
